subject: Study Skills
title: Lecture 7 – Tips for Good Study Habits

A.q: What is the first study habit tip?
options: Highlight every line as you read
Set a regular time to study
A.explain: The first tip is to process information as deeply as possible. Highlighting while reading can become mindless. Saving practice for the night before is not advised. Setting a regular time is a study-atmosphere tip.

A.q: What does elaboration help you do?
options: Use practice exams to guide studying
Link information to what you know
Formulate questions to maintain reading focus
Layer major concepts before smaller details
A.explain: Elaboration helps memory by linking information to what you already know. Practice exams guide studying, questions maintain focus, and layering organizes concepts.

A.q: How should you organize studying by layering?
A.explain: Layering means learning major concepts first, then big categories, then headings and subheadings. Details-first, headings-first, and subheadings-first reverse the order.

A.q: What should you do with practice exams and questions from study aids?
options: Save them for the night before the exam
Use them to guide your studying
Skip them when preparing for exams
Review them after the exam has ended
A.explain: Practice exams and questions from study aids should guide studying while you study. They should not be saved for the night before the exam.

A.q: When studying practice questions, what should you examine?
options: The right answers and the stem
The wrong answers and the stem
A.explain: Look at both right and wrong answers for clues about what is important to study. The stem, title, or instructions do not give the same answer-pattern clues.

A.q: When should you highlight while reading?
options: As you read each line quickly
After finishing a paragraph or section
Before opening the assigned textbook chapter
On the title and cover page
A.explain: Highlight after finishing a paragraph or section, then think about the most important information and go back to highlight it. Line-by-line highlighting can become mindless.

A.q: What does formulating questions do while reading?
options: It gives a purpose and helps focus.
It prevents prediction of exam questions.
A.explain: Formulating questions is an active reading strategy. It gives a purpose for reading, raises curiosity, increases comprehension, and helps maintain focus.

A.q: When can you write questions for active reading?
A.explain: Write questions before you read, as you read, and after you read. The other timing patterns miss part of the active reading strategy.

A.q: What is the first step of SQ4R?
A.explain: SQ4R starts with surveying the chapter. Reciting, reviewing, and recording are later steps.

A.q: Which set lists the SQ4R steps in order?
options: Survey, Read, Question, Record, Recite, Review
Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Record, Review
Survey, Question, Read, Record, Recite, Review
Survey, Question, Read, Record, Review, Recite
A.explain: The order is Survey, Question, Read, Record, Recite, Review. Each wrong option swaps one step position, making the sequence incorrect.

A.q: What is the first essential strategy for textbook reading?
A.explain: The first essential strategy is a clear intention to understand what you read. Organized systems, inquisitiveness, and time management are other essential strategies.

A.q: What should you relate new information to?
A.explain: Relate new information to existing schemas in long-term memory. Sensory codes, headings, and glossary or index entries are other reading or surveying tools.

A.q: Which textbook part lists the chapters and page numbers?
A.explain: The table of contents lists chapters and page numbers. An appendix adds material, a glossary defines terms, and an index locates topics.

A.q: What should you read carefully when surveying a chapter?
A.explain: Read introductory material carefully. Headings, visuals, marginal notes, terminology, and end-of-chapter items are also surveyed, but the advice singles out introductory material.

A.q: How should you begin reading science textbooks?
options: Use thorough reading from the start
A.explain: Begin with overview reading, then use thorough reading. Examples, terminology, mental images, recitation, diagrams, and larger concepts come later.

A.q: How long should pre-reading take?
A.explain: Pre-reading should involve basic skimming and take about 10-15 minutes. Two hours, five minutes, or the entire night do not match the stated time.

A.q: Where should you sit during class?
A.explain: Sit where distractions will be minimized. Talking friends, the back row, and phone checking increase distractions.

A.q: When should you review notes after class?
A.explain: Briefly review notes within a day or two. Waiting a month, never reviewing, or reviewing during the exam does not follow the timing.

A.q: What should you form for class?
A.explain: Form a good listening habit. Talking, daydreaming, and phone checking prevent listening.

A.q: What should you avoid for studying?
A.explain: Try not to use your bed for studying so it stays linked to relaxation. A clear desk, good lighting, and a proper chair support studying.

A.q: What should a study desk have on it?
A.explain: The desk should have nothing on it except the subject you are studying. Unrelated objects, snacks, drinks, and phones create distractions.

A.q: Which items are listed as necessary for studying?
options: Soft bed, good lighting, chair, books, supplies, clock, drink
Solid surface, good lighting, chair, books, supplies, clock, drink
Solid surface, good lighting, phone, books, supplies, clock, drink
Solid surface, good lighting, chair, books, supplies, clock, snacks
A.explain: The listed items are a solid surface, good lighting, a chair, books, supplies, a clock, and a drink. A soft bed, a phone, and snacks replace required items.

A.q: Is your best friend the best study partner?
A.explain: Your best friend is not necessarily your best study partner. A different partner may give a new perspective. A guaranteed choice, identical partner, and avoiding discussion do not match.

A.q: What should a real break include?
options: Check your phone the whole time
A.explain: Make sure a break is really a break. Get up, go outside, and walk around. Staying seated, checking the phone, or continuing to read does not make a real break.

A.q: Which set lists everyday brain foods?
A.explain: Everyday brain foods listed include breakfast, oranges, water, healthy snacks, eggs, fish, berries, raisins, chocolate/crisps, and nuts. The other sets are not the listed everyday brain-food set.

A.q: What should you do if you cannot focus on reading?
options: Sit and stare at the book
Do an easier task then retry
A.explain: Do something a bit easier or more enjoyable, then try again in 30 minutes. Sitting and staring, giving up, or checking the phone does not ease you back into studying.

A.q: What is a mind map?
A.explain: A mind map is a diagram used to visually organize information. It is hierarchical and shows relationships among pieces of the whole. A list, paragraph, or numerical table is not a mind map.

A.q: Who are mind maps especially good for?
A.explain: Mind maps are good for the visual learner. They are used to visualize, structure, and classify ideas. Auditory, kinesthetic, and no learner do not match the statement.

A.q: Which is a study technique?
A.explain: Study difficult subjects first. Also use waiting time effectively and use a regular study area day after day. Easy-first, sleeping area, and ignored gaps go against the techniques.

A.q: Where should you study?
A.explain: Study where you will be alert. Do not study where you sleep, in noisy areas, or while using the phone. The library can also signal work mode.

A.q: What should you hang on your door?
A.explain: Hang a do not disturb sign on your door. A come in anytime sign, a phone is on sign, or a no studying sign would invite interruptions or prevent study.

A.q: Which set lists the keys to study?
options: Time management, daydreaming, note taking, focus
Excuses, mind maps, note taking, focus
Time management, mind maps, note taking, focus
Time management, mind maps, phone use, focus
A.explain: The keys are time management, mind maps, note taking, and concentration. Daydreaming, excuses, and phone use are distractions, not keys.

A.q: Use the SQ4R sequence.

steps.prompt: What is the first SQ4R step?
After Survey, what is the next SQ4R step?
After Question, what is the next SQ4R step?
After Read, what is the next SQ4R step?
After Record, what is the next SQ4R step?
After Recite, what is the final SQ4R step?

A.explain: SQ4R order is Survey, Question, Read, Record, Recite, Review. Survey is first; Question follows Survey; Read follows Question; Record follows Read; Recite follows Record; Review is final.

A.q: What should you stop looking for?
A.explain: Stop looking for excuses not to study. Think about the end goal, your exam. Free time, lighting, and quieter places are useful adjustments, not excuses.

A.q: How can you use dead time?
A.explain: Think about dead time and use it more effectively for studying. Sleep, phone use, or leaving it unused does not use it effectively.

A.q: What should you know to prepare well?
A.explain: Know the exam papers and review mock exam papers. The paper title, one sample question, or no exam knowledge does not prepare you fully.

A.q: What is the key to study?
options: Learning to be a smart learner
A.explain: The key to study is learning to be a smart learner, especially with exam questions and exam papers. Avoiding preparation, studying once, or ignoring time management is the opposite.

A.q: What do questions and answers create?
A.explain: Questions and answers create memory cues or associations to recall information later. They do not create confusion, boredom, or distraction.

A.q: What should you do with notes after class?
A.explain: Reorganize, restate, and reformat notes to process information at a deeper level. Leaving them unchanged, throwing them away, or reading them once does not deepen processing.

A.q: Why should you note your caffeine intake?
A.explain: Note caffeine intake so you can keep alert without becoming jittery and stop in time to sleep. Hunger, outdoor breaks, and bed-relaxation are separate study-habit tips.

A.q: Which situation illustrates using waiting time?
A.explain: Use waiting time effectively, such as waiting for the bus or time between classes. Long blocks, late nights, or ignored gaps waste usable time.

A.q: What should you agree with family about?
A.explain: Agree with family or friends about suitable study time. No scheduled study time, phone time, or banned quiet time would prevent studying.

A.q: What should good study habits help you remember?
A.explain: With good study habits, you should remember your predicted results. Excuses, distractions, and phone numbers are not the stated outcome.

A.q: Which approach divides learning into separate sessions?
A.explain: Spaced studying means learning across separate sessions. Timetable planning, use of waiting time, and regular study time are other ways to manage study time.

A.q: Which set lists study techniques?
options: Deep processing, waiting time, regular study area, library signal
Difficult subject first, mind maps, regular study area, library signal
Difficult subject first, waiting time, highlight sections, library signal
Difficult subject first, waiting time, regular study area, library signal
A.explain: Study techniques include difficult subjects first, waiting time, regular study areas, and library signals. Deep processing, mind maps, and highlighting belong to other study tips.

A.q: Which set lists how to get the best possible results?
options: Predicted results, exam papers, study timetable
Smart learning, do-not-disturb sign, study timetable
Smart learning, exam papers, study timetable
Smart learning, exam papers, brain foods
A.explain: The best-results advice is smart learning with exam papers, plus using time effectively by making a study timetable. Predicted results, do-not-disturb signs, and brain foods belong to other sections.

A.q: Which set lists ways to use your time wisely?
options: Do-not-disturb sign, exam timetable, dead time, mock papers
Study timetable, brain foods, dead time, mock papers
Study timetable, exam timetable, elaboration, mock papers
Study timetable, exam timetable, dead time, mock papers
A.explain: Using time wisely includes study and exam timetables, dead time, and mock papers. Do-not-disturb signs, brain foods, and elaboration belong to other tips.

A.q: Which set lists the first four study habit tips?
options: Social studying, reading, lectures, study atmosphere
Processing, reading, brain foods, study atmosphere
A.explain: The first four main tips are processing, reading, lectures, and study atmosphere. Social studying, highlighting, and brain foods are not first-level tips.

A.q: Which set lists points for surveying a chapter?
options: Copyright page, headings, visuals, end-of-chapter items
Introductory material, headings, visuals, the bibliography
Introductory material, headings, appendix, end-of-chapter items
Introductory material, headings, visuals, end-of-chapter items
A.explain: Chapter surveying includes introductory material, headings, visuals, marginal notes, terminology, and end-of-chapter items. Copyright pages, bibliographies, and appendices belong to textbook surveying.

A.q: Which set lists parts for surveying a textbook?
options: Chapter headings, copyright page, glossary, index
Title page, chapter visuals, glossary, index
Title page, copyright page, end-of-chapter items, index
Title page, copyright page, glossary, index
A.explain: Textbook surveying includes the title page, copyright page, table of contents, introductory information, appendix, glossary, references, and index. Chapter headings, visuals, and end-of-chapter items belong to chapter surveying.

A.q: What does liaising with classmates help you do?
A.explain: Liaising with classmates helps you get, swap, or share notes. A new perspective comes from a different partner, websites are another help source, and answering machines relate to phone interruptions.

A.q: After Survey and Question, which set lists the 4 Rs in order?
A.explain: SQ4R begins with Survey and Question, then the 4 Rs are Read, Record, Recite, and Review. The wrong options place one R too early or too late.

A.q: What does liaise mean when classmates help each other?
options: Visually organize information in a diagram
A.explain: Liaise means to work together and exchange information. When classmates help each other, this includes getting, swapping, or sharing notes. Linking information describes elaboration, identical partners relates to study partners, and diagrams describe mind maps.

A.q: Which elaboration method reorganizes information?
A.explain: Elaboration includes linking information to prior knowledge, reorganizing with charts, outlines, or diagrams, using vivid visualization, and acting out situations. This item tests the reorganizing method.

A.q: What do practice questions show you?
options: When to take a real break
Where to read or watch more
Why to use a mind map
A.explain: Practice questions show where you need to read or watch more. Layering, breaks, and mind maps are other study-habit tips.

A.q: What should you do after finishing a section?
A.explain: After finishing a section, predict possible exam questions, their wording, correct answers, and misleading answers. Spaced studying, liaising, and memory cues are other tips.

A.q: Use the pre-lecture preparation steps.

steps.prompt: What should you pre-read before lecture?
After pre-reading major concepts, how long should skimming take?
After skimming for 10-15 minutes, what should you understand?
After understanding new words, what should you identify?
After identifying difficult points, what should you plan?

A.explain: Pre-lecture preparation moves from major concepts to 10-15 minute skimming, new words, difficult points, and note organization. Other durations, later items, highlighting, breaks, and seating are not the asked step.

A.q: Use the after-lecture note steps.

steps.prompt: What should you mark in notes after lecture?
After marking clear points and clarification needs, what should you cross-reference?

A.explain: After class, mark clear points and clarification needs; predicted results, brain foods, and library signals are other tips. Then cross-reference notes with lectures, books, and aids; headings, charts, and glossary entries are other tools.

A.q: Use the science-textbook facts.

steps.prompt: What does understanding science textbooks involve?
After hands-on lab demonstrations, what does the material use?

A.explain: Understanding science textbooks involves hands-on laboratory demonstrations, experiments, and observations. Science textbooks also use declarative and procedural knowledge. Major concepts, charts, and sensory codes are other tips.

A.q: Match each social-studying helper to its purpose.
A.explain: Social studying includes swapping notes with classmates, gaining a new perspective from a different partner, and asking teachers or looking up websites.

A.q: What should you track for body needs?
A.explain: Track when you get hungry and what gives an energy boost so you can plan snacks and meal breaks. Break timing, caffeine and water, and meal or sleep planning are other body-needs points.

A.q: Why choose the right food and drink?
A.explain: Right food and drink aid concentration during exams. Organizing charts, memory cues, and reading focus are other study strategies.

A.q: Which task suits the evening for a morning person?
A.explain: A morning person should study the hardest material in the morning and keep evenings for lower-attention tasks such as making flashcards or rewriting charts. Lab demonstrations and mock papers belong to other sections.

A.q: What should you do with mock exam papers?
A.explain: Review mock exam papers and spend time redoing answers. Saving them for exam night, sticking timetables above tables, and predicting misleading answers are other tips.

A.q: Which set lists uses of mind maps?
options: Visualize, organize, solve problems, make predictions, structure answers
Visualize, highlight, solve problems, make decisions, structure answers
Visualize, organize, wait for buses, make decisions, structure answers
Visualize, organize, solve problems, make decisions, structure answers
A.explain: Mind maps are used to visualize, organize information, solve problems, support decision making, and help structure answers. Predictions, highlighting, and waiting time are other study topics.

A.q: Match each essential reading strategy to its description.
A.explain: Essential reading strategies include using an organized system, being inquisitive, including feedback, managing reading time, and encoding ordinary words into new sensory codes.
